pool: Most {service} work in {place} starts with the fire risk assessment. The Regulatory Reform (Fire Safety) Order 2005 puts the duty on the responsible person, and the assessment is where gaps in {subject_l} usually first get written down. Send us the current assessment and we scope the work against what it actually says.

Before anyone attends a {place} site we ask for the address, the building use, the number of storeys and any recent certificates. That lets the engineer arrive with the right parts and access kit, and it keeps the first visit to a survey rather than a guess.

Occupied buildings in {place} need work planned around the people inside them. We agree isolation times, escape-route cover and any fire watch with the site contact before work starts, so the building is never left without protection that the assessment relies on.

Purpose-built blocks of flats over 11 metres fall under the Fire Safety (England) Regulations 2022, which added duties on wayfinding signage, fire door checks and information for the fire and rescue service. If your {place} building is in scope, we can tie the {subject_l} work into those checks.

Houses in multiple occupation in {place} are licensed by the council, and licence conditions often name fire detection, emergency lighting and fire doors. We read the licence conditions alongside the fire risk assessment so the work closes the items the council will look for.

Care homes, schools and surgeries in and around {place} usually need work done out of hours or in phased sections. We plan the programme with the manager on site, keep a written log of what was isolated and when, and hand back each area in working order before we move on.

Every visit ends with written records: what was tested or installed, what was found, and what still needs doing. Keep those records with the fire safety logbook. They are what an inspecting fire officer, insurer or managing agent will ask to see.

Where a defect is found in {place} we explain it plainly and say whether it affects the building's fire strategy now or can wait for planned works. Remedial work is quoted separately in writing, so nothing is added to the job without your agreement.

Commercial units in {place}, such as shops, offices, workshops and warehouses, each have their own fire strategy, often set when the unit was fitted out. We work to that strategy and the original drawings where they exist, and flag anywhere later alterations have broken it.

Managing agents with several {place} buildings can group visits into one planned round. Each building still gets its own records and findings, but travel and access are arranged once, which makes it easier to keep every site on its inspection dates.

Fire protection systems depend on each other. Detection triggers alarms, alarms may release hold-open doors and open smoke vents, and emergency lighting carries people out. When we work on {subject_l} in {place} we check the links to the rest of the system as well as the item itself.

Older {place} buildings often have mixed equipment from several installers. We record what is there, its age and condition, and whether spares are still available, so you can plan replacement before a part fails and cannot be sourced.

Access matters on {place} jobs: keys, codes, roof hatches, plant rooms and tenant notice. Tell us what notice your residents or tenants need and we will fit the visit around it. Flats usually need written notice before we enter individual homes.

For new installations and major alterations in {place}, building control may need to see the design and the completion certificates. We supply the paperwork in the form the council or approved inspector expects, so sign-off is not held up at the end of a fit-out.

Insurers increasingly ask for evidence of fire protection maintenance at renewal. A current service record for {subject_l}, with dates and engineer details, answers that question quickly and avoids the policy conditions being queried after a claim.

Quotes for {place} are price on application. Once we know the building, the scope and the access, you get a written quote that lists what is included, how long it should take and what records you will receive at the end.

If your {place} building has had a fire, a false alarm problem or an enforcement notice, tell us when you get in touch. We prioritise work that closes a legal or safety gap, and we can write the scope so it answers the specific points raised.

Residents and staff are part of fire safety. After work in {place} we can explain to the site contact what changed, what the regular user checks are and who to call if something looks wrong, so the building is looked after between our visits.

Contractors working near fire protection in {place} buildings, such as electricians, joiners and decorators, can damage it without meaning to. Painted door seals, blocked detectors and cables through compartment walls are common finds. We note them so they can be put right.

Where a {place} building is being refurbished, it is cheaper to plan {subject_l} into the works than to retrofit afterwards. Share the programme early and we can say what needs doing at first fix, what at second fix and what at handover.

Small landlords in {place} with one or two properties have the same duties as large portfolios, just on a smaller scale. We keep the scope proportionate to the building, and we will tell you when something is not needed rather than adding it to the quote.

Your fire safety logbook should show a steady pattern of checks, servicing and remedial work. If the {place} logbook has gaps, we can carry out a baseline inspection and start the record afresh from that date.

We are based in Offerton, Stockport and plan work across the UK mainland. Visits to {place} are booked as planned daytime appointments unless the site needs out-of-hours access, and travel is shown on the written quote.

specific.fire-alarms: Fire alarm systems are designed, installed and serviced to BS 5839-1 for non-domestic buildings and BS 5839-6 for homes. The standard expects servicing at intervals of no more than six months in most premises, with a weekly user test of a different call point each time.
specific.emergency-lighting: Emergency lighting is designed and tested to BS 5266-1. That means a short monthly function test and a full-duration test once a year, both written in the logbook, with failed fittings and batteries replaced and the test repeated.
specific.fire-signage: Safety signs follow BS ISO 7010 symbols, with BS 5499 guidance on escape route signage. A sign has to be visible from where people will need it, readable under emergency lighting, and consistent across the building so the route is never ambiguous.
specific.fire-extinguishers: Portable extinguishers are selected, sited and serviced to BS 5306-8 and BS 5306-3. A basic service is due every year, with extended servicing or discharge testing at the intervals the standard sets for each type.
specific.evacuation-alerts: Evacuation alert systems for blocks of flats are covered by BS 8629. They let the fire and rescue service sound an evacuation signal in all or part of a building that normally runs a stay-put strategy.
specific.fire-doors: Fire doors are only as good as their weakest part: leaf, frame, gaps, seals, hinges, closer and glazing. Inspections follow the manufacturer's certification and BS 8214 guidance, and flat entrance doors in larger blocks have their own checking intervals under the 2022 regulations.
specific.fire-risk-assessments: A fire risk assessment looks at the hazards, the people at risk, the existing precautions and the management of the building. It should be reviewed regularly and whenever the building, its use or its occupants change significantly.
specific.dry-risers: Dry rising mains are maintained to BS 9990. That calls for a visual inspection every six months and a wet pressure test once a year, with inlet and landing valves, boxes and signage checked at the same time.
specific.sprinkler-systems: Sprinkler systems are designed and maintained to BS EN 12845 for commercial buildings and BS 9251 for residential and domestic buildings. Weekly checks are done on site, with quarterly and annual inspections by a competent engineer.
specific.fire-stopping: Fire stopping seals gaps where services pass through fire-resisting walls and floors. Each seal has to be a tested product, installed to its manufacturer's details for that size of opening and type of service, and recorded so the next contractor can see what is there.
specific.fire-compartmentation: Compartmentation keeps fire and smoke in the space where they start. A compartmentation survey checks walls, floors, ceilings, risers and roof voids for breaches, and records each defect with its location so it can be fixed and signed off.
specific.fire-suppression: Fixed fire suppression covers gaseous, water-mist and foam systems protecting server rooms, plant and storage. Gaseous systems follow BS EN 15004 and need room integrity testing, so a suppression visit checks the enclosure as well as the cylinders and the control panel.
specific.kitchen-fire-suppression: Commercial kitchen suppression protects the canopy, plenum, duct and cooking appliances with a wet chemical agent. Systems are tested to LPS 1223, linked to the gas shut-off, and serviced at least every six months alongside regular duct and filter cleaning.
specific.aov-air-handling: Automatic opening vents and smoke shafts keep stairs and corridors clear of smoke so people can escape and firefighters can get in. Systems follow BS EN 12101 for the components and BS 7346-8 for the design, and need regular functional testing and a full annual service.
specific.smoke-co-alarms: Smoke and carbon monoxide alarms in rented homes fall under the Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Alarm (Amendment) Regulations 2022. Landlords need a smoke alarm on every storey used as living space and a CO alarm in any room with a fixed combustion appliance, tested at the start of each tenancy.
